shots: a small apartment kitchen at night, a rent notice on the table, a 39 year old African American mother with brown skin and long braids pulled back, wearing a work polo shirt sitting with her phone on speaker and her head in her hand, warm overhead light, no readable text

shots.en: Girl, rent down here is half. Bring the kids. The schools are fine. I've got the back rooms ready.
I know. I know. Let me talk to them.

shots: a 15 year old African American boy, very tall and broad shouldered, with short twists, wearing a football practice jersey standing still in a dim hallway with a gym bag over his shoulder, overhearing a conversation from the kitchen, worried face

shots.en: I heard every word from the hallway. I was still in my practice gear.

shots: a small classic diner booth at night, two hot dogs with chili and a basket of fries on the table, a 39 year old African American mother with brown skin and long braids pulled back, wearing a work polo shirt across from a 15 year old African American boy, very tall and broad shouldered, with short twists, wearing a football practice jersey who is not eating, an 8 year old African American boy with a round face beside him

shots.en: Say it.
I got three seasons left, Mama. Three. Coach got me starting both ways. My boys...
Your boys will understand.
It ain't about them understanding. I said I'd be there. If I leave, I'm the jit who quit on 'em.
And if we stay, I might be the mama who can't make rent.

shots: a high school football practice field in the afternoon, a 55 year old African American football coach with a gray goatee, wearing a team windbreaker and cap talking to a 15 year old African American boy, very tall and broad shouldered, with short twists, wearing a football practice jersey in pads beside a blocking sled, serious conversation

shots.en: You've been hitting like you're mad at the sled.
We might move.
Hm. You know what you're worth to this team?
I know what I'm worth to my mama. She's tired, Coach.
Then don't make her carry this by herself. Tell her what you're willing to do, not just what you want.

shots: a small living room in the evening, a 15 year old African American boy, very tall and broad shouldered, with short twists, wearing a football practice jersey sitting forward on the edge of a couch speaking earnestly to a 39 year old African American mother with brown skin and long braids pulled back, wearing a work polo shirt, three younger siblings on the floor, an 8 year old African American boy with a round face grinning

shots.en: If we stay, I'll get a job Saturdays. I'll watch Dre after school so you can take the second shift. I'll cut grass on the whole block.
You're fifteen.
I'm fifteen and six-three. People pay big dudes to carry stuff.
I'll carry small stuff.
Let me pray on it. For real. Not just say it.

shots: a 39 year old African American mother with brown skin and long braids pulled back, wearing a work polo shirt alone at a kitchen table at 2 in the morning, a Bible open in front of her and a rent notice beside it, a single light, whispering a prayer with her eyes closed

shots.en: Lord, I don't want to raise him to stay when it hurts, and I don't want to raise him to quit when it's hard. Show me which this is.
Seek the peace of the city, for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.

shots: moving day at a smaller house one block from a high school, a 15 year old African American boy, very tall and broad shouldered, with short twists, wearing a football practice jersey carrying a couch by himself up the front steps, moving boxes, neighbors watching and smiling, afternoon sun

shots.en: We found a smaller place, closer to the school. Marcus kept every promise. The rent is still tight. But we're here.

shots: Friday night high school football under stadium lights, a 15 year old African American boy, very tall and broad shouldered, with short twists, wearing a football practice jersey in full uniform on the line looking up at the stands, a 39 year old African American mother with brown skin and long braids pulled back, wearing a work polo shirt in the stands wearing his jersey beside an 8 year old African American boy with a round face, cheering

shots.en: Mama stayed for me. So every Friday, I play for her.
A man's heart deviseth his way: but the Lord directeth his steps. Proverbs sixteen, nine.

shots: a 39 year old African American mother with brown skin and long braids pulled back, wearing a work polo shirt sitting on her front steps at dusk looking at her phone with a calm small smile, no readable text

shots.en: Stay or go, you don't have to decide alone.
In Community Covenant, tap Ask for Help and write what you're carrying. A real person from our team writes back the same day, with the Word and a next step.
Every morning it reads Scripture over you, with gospel music, and walks you into prayer.
Get Community Covenant at covenant dot crispusmundo dot com. You are not alone.

shots: a bright kitchen in the afternoon, a 38 year old African American woman with brown skin and short natural hair, wearing a gray work shirt on her phone grinning and mouthing excitedly to a 13 year old African American girl with long braids at the counter

shots.en: We're excited to have you. You'll get a barcode for the screening. Just get it done.
Yes, ma'am. Monday, Wednesday, Friday. I'll be there.

shots: a 38 year old African American woman with brown skin and short natural hair, wearing a gray work shirt in a busy home holding a sick child on her hip while talking on the phone, school papers and a calendar on the fridge, chaotic morning light

shots.en: Then came three days. A sick kid. A school meeting. A ride that fell through. The email with the code sat unopened under fifteen others.

shots: a medical clinic front counter, a clinic worker shaking her head kindly, a 38 year old African American woman with brown skin and short natural hair, wearing a gray work shirt holding up her phone, stunned, fluorescent light, no readable text

shots.en: I'm sorry. This code expired yesterday.
Can you... can it be reissued?
That has to come from the employer.

shots: a 38 year old African American woman with brown skin and short natural hair, wearing a gray work shirt sitting in her parked car in a clinic parking lot gripping the steering wheel with both hands, phone on speaker on the dashboard, holding back tears

shots.en: Unfortunately we can't extend it. You're welcome to reapply in three months.

shots: a 38 year old African American woman with brown skin and short natural hair, wearing a gray work shirt at a kitchen table at 2 in the morning, a laptop open and a Bible beside it, her phone glowing in her hand, the house dark and quiet, no readable text

shots.en: I did everything right except three days. Three days, Lord.
I have set before thee an open door, and no man can shut it.
Then open it. Because I can't.

shots: a 13 year old African American girl with long braids in pajamas sitting beside a 38 year old African American woman with brown skin and short natural hair, wearing a gray work shirt at the kitchen table at night, resting her head on her mother's shoulder, a phone glowing on the table

shots.en: My daughter came down in her pajamas. She didn't say a word. She just put her head on my shoulder.

shots: morning kitchen, a 38 year old African American woman with brown skin and short natural hair, wearing a gray work shirt answering her ringing phone with surprise, coffee mug in her other hand, sunlight through the window

shots.en: Danielle? I saw what happened. That wasn't right. I'm reissuing your order. Can you go today?
Today. Yes. Today.
Go! I got the kids!

shots: a 38 year old African American woman with brown skin and short natural hair, wearing a gray work shirt sitting in her car smiling with tears in her eyes, reading a text on her phone, morning light, no readable text

shots.en: A week later, a text. Results are in. Can you start Monday?
I'd love to tell you I believed the whole time. I didn't. I just kept the app open and my daughter's head on my shoulder. Sometimes that's all the faith you've got. It was enough.
Behold, I have set before thee an open door, and no man can shut it. Revelation three, eight.

shots: close-up of a woman's hands holding a smartphone at a dark kitchen table at night, the screen glowing softly, a Bible beside it, no readable text

shots.en: Up at 2 A.M. with a closed door? Press play.
Community Covenant reads Scripture over you, with gospel music, even on the nights you don't feel like praying.
Tap Ask for Help, and a real person from our team writes back the same day.
Get Community Covenant at covenant dot crispusmundo dot com. You are not alone.

shots: a high school football locker room, a coach in a team polo addressing players sitting on benches, a 15 year old African American high school football player, tall and strong, with short hair staring at his phone while teammates text excitedly

shots.en: Friday's Salute to Service. Every one of you picks somebody who served. They'll be on the sideline at the anthem. You walk over and salute them.

shots: a 15 year old African American high school football player, tall and strong, with short hair in his bedroom at night on a video call, the phone screen showing a 42 year old African American man in a dark blue US Navy working uniform standing on the deck of a Navy ship with wind blowing

shots.en: Friday? Man... I'm on watch, son. I can't get there.
It's cool.
It's not cool, and you know it's not cool. But I'll be on that stream. Pick somebody who earned it. Make it count.

shots: a family kitchen in the evening, a 15 year old African American high school football player, tall and strong, with short hair leaning on the counter talking with a 38 year old African American mother with shoulder length hair who is cooking

shots.en: Mom, who do I salute?
Who in your life served and showed up for you?
Deacon Hollis drives me to church when you're working Sundays.
Then ask him. Like a man. In person.

shots: the front porch of a small brick house in the afternoon, a 15 year old African American high school football player, tall and strong, with short hair standing respectfully on the steps, a 74 year old African American Army veteran with white hair and glasses, wearing an old olive Army cap and holding a wooden cane sitting in a porch chair looking out at the street, moved

shots.en: Deacon, would you stand for me Friday? At the salute.
Forty-nine years since anybody saluted me. Yes, son. I'll stand.

shots: Friday night high school football stadium under bright lights during the anthem, a 15 year old African American high school football player, tall and strong, with short hair in full pads giving a sharp military salute to a 74 year old African American Army veteran with white hair and glasses, wearing an old olive Army cap and holding a wooden cane standing on the sideline without his cane, saluting back, the crowd standing

shots.en: He set his cane down and stood on his own. When he saluted me back, his hand was shaking.

shots: fourth quarter of a night football game, a 15 year old African American high school football player, tall and strong, with short hair limping slightly then lining back up in a three point stance, stadium lights, determined

shots.en: Show up. Stay disciplined. Go hard.

shots: after a night football game on the field, a 15 year old African American high school football player, tall and strong, with short hair laughing holding his phone up on a video call while teammates crowd around laughing, stadium lights

shots.en: Jordan! Jordan! I saw you limp, and I saw you line back up! That's my son!
Dad, you're doing it again. Like when you walked me to practice and yelled my name down the whole block.
And I'll keep doing it till you're forty! Tell the Deacon thank you for me. He stood where I couldn't.
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works. Ephesians two, ten.

shots: a 15 year old African American high school football player, tall and strong, with short hair sitting on a bench in a gym in the morning, sweaty after a workout, looking at his phone with a Bible beside him, no readable text

shots.en: Show up. Stay disciplined. Go hard, in the Word too.
Community Covenant gives you Scripture, prayer and a daily workout on the same page, every day for thirty days.
Tap Ask for Help, and a real person from our team writes back the same day.
Get Community Covenant at covenant dot crispusmundo dot com. You are not alone.

shots: a quiet kitchen at 2 in the morning, a cake box on the counter with two gold number one candles, a 42 year old African American woman with brown skin and her hair in a soft low bun sitting alone at the table holding a framed photo of an older man in a church suit, a single warm light

shots.en: Tomorrow my twins turn eleven on the eleventh. Their golden birthday. And every year, the week before it, I go quiet.

shots: soft focus memory of a hospital hallway, a 31 year old African American woman, heavily pregnant with twins with one hand on her belly and one hand on the wall, pale light, film grain

shots.en: Eleven years ago, on the second, my Father went home to God. I was carrying twins. I had three little ones at home. And the family I needed most wasn't all there for me.

shots: soft memory of a graveside in light rain, a 31 year old African American woman, heavily pregnant with twins standing in a black dress, someone holding an umbrella over her, mourners in dark coats, film grain

shots.en: On the ninth, we buried him. I remember thinking: I can't hold one more thing.

shots: memory of a hospital delivery room, a 31 year old African American woman, heavily pregnant with twins in a hospital bed crying and laughing at once, two tiny newborn twins wrapped in blankets, monitors, warm light, film grain

shots.en: On the eleventh, two days later, my body said, now. They came early. Small. Loud. Alive.

shots: a 42 year old African American woman with brown skin and her hair in a soft low bun at the kitchen table at night gently touching a framed photo, an old Bible open in front of her with a worn underlined page, warm lamp light

shots.en: For a long time I thought that week broke me. Grief, a funeral and two babies in nine days.
But I've had eleven years to look at it. That week didn't break me. It prepared me. I had already walked through water and fire in nine days, and God was there in every one of them.
When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee.

shots: a bright morning kitchen, an 11 year old African American boy and girl twins racing in excitedly in pajamas, a birthday cake with two gold number one candles lit, a 42 year old African American woman with brown skin and her hair in a soft low bun smiling

shots.en: Is that for Grandpa again?
Every year.
Can we sing to him too?

shots: a small slice of birthday cake on a plate beside a framed photo of an older man in a church suit, a 42 year old African American woman with brown skin and her hair in a soft low bun and her 11 year old twins singing together around a kitchen table in morning light

shots.en: Sad and glad in the same week. God never asked me to pick one.
A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance. Ecclesiastes three, four.

shots: a 42 year old African American woman with brown skin and her hair in a soft low bun sitting on a couch in the evening with a phone in her hand and a cup of tea, a calm small smile, no readable text

shots.en: Grieving and celebrating in the same week? You're not alone.
In Community Covenant, the Wisdom Reels walk you through grief and healing with Scripture read aloud.
Tap Ask for Help, and a real person from our team writes back the same day and prays with you.
Get Community Covenant at covenant dot crispusmundo dot com. You are not alone.
